claims.text: Hafnium is a carbide- and nitride-forming alloying element.
Adding a minor fraction of hafnium to a refractory high-entropy alloy promotes in situ formation of fine, thermally stable carbide dispersoids.
The carbide dispersoids produced by minor hafnium addition enhance high-temperature strength.
Minor hafnium addition and carbide formation minimally affect alloy density.
Minor hafnium addition and carbide formation preserve room-temperature mechanical performance.
Adding approximately 1–3 at.% hafnium followed by controlled high-temperature heat treatment will precipitate nanoscale HfC or HfN particles.
The resulting HfC or HfN dispersoids will be distributed both along grain boundaries and within grains.
Stable carbide or nitride particles impede dislocation motion at high temperatures.
Stable carbide or nitride particles retard grain-boundary sliding at high temperatures.
Impeded dislocation motion and retarded grain-boundary sliding improve creep resistance.
The hafnium-alloyed and heat-treated material will have higher yield strength or creep resistance at 800–1000 °C than the baseline alloy.
The room-temperature mechanical properties of the hafnium-modified material will remain comparable to those of the baseline alloy.
The beneficial effect is restricted to hafnium contents in the low atomic-percent range, approximately 1–3 at.%.
Higher hafnium additions could produce excessive coarse particles.
Higher hafnium additions could increase alloy density.
Excessive coarse-particle formation at higher hafnium contents could degrade room-temperature properties.
Dispersoid size and distribution depend on heat-treatment parameters.
